body.text: In short:
Bupa emailed GPs working at one of its clinics, encouraging increased billing of chronic condition management plans, which cost more than standard appointments.
Senior doctors say they are concerned corporatised GP practices are prioritising profit over patient care, but Bupa defended the email.
What's next?
The Department of Health says it is spending $147 million over four years to review the industry and improve compliance.
A GP clinic operated by health insurance giant Bupa encouraged doctors to lift their billing of more costly Medicare items.
The ABC has obtained an email from a Bupa clinic to its GPs in June, which told doctors to ensure "revenue is increasing".
The email asked doctors to do this by increasing the bookings of patients for costly Medicare checks known as "chronic condition management plans" (CCMPs).
It further encouraged doctors to re-book patients, if they were eligible for further checks but Medicare rules prevented them from being claimed on the same day.
CCMPs are personalised plans written by GPs, designed to create a structure to improve outcomes for people struggling with complex health conditions.
The plans can be used for conditions ranging from eczema to heart disease, and while often beneficial to patients, they may not be essential for everyone with a chronic condition.
The Medicare schedule fee for a GP to prepare a CCMP is $160.60, compared to $87.10 for a standard GP appointment lasting at least 20 minutes.
The federal government's spending on the plans is rising rapidly and it is now spending nearly $1.3 billion a year on these chronic care plans out of the $35 billion Medicare budget.
'Need to explain' why items not billed

In the email, Bupa told doctors their appointment books were closely scrutinised each day through the popular software portal Cubiko, for "possible service opportunities", and notes were left about what could be billed.
The booking software includes a specific function to check for chances to bill patients for 'possible service opportunities', including the costly chronic care plans.
The email also detailed how the "ops team" had tasked the practice managers with "ensuring revenue is increasing by ensuring there is an uptick in billings of HA [health assessments]".
Bupa's email then went on to list the Medicare item numbers for these health assessments, including chronic condition management plans and a nurse item.

GPs were reminded that practice managers need to "ensure" an increase in patients being charged for these more expensive Medicare items, otherwise practice managers "need to explain why these are not being billed".
In a statement, Bupa said the email was sent at one clinic and was an attempt to remind doctors to consider preventative care.
"Patient needs, clinical judgement and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first," it said.
"While technology solutions help provide prompts … decisions about a patient's care and eligibility always remain with the treating doctor."

Bupa said practice managers provide "administrative support to our doctors. Patient needs, clinical judgement, and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first and we reinforce this through ongoing guidance and training".
If GPs coerced, 'it has to be stopped'
Health economist Terry Barnes was a senior adviser to two health ministers in the Howard government.
He told the ABC he was not surprised by Bupa's email, and it was a window into how much corporate owners of GP clinics "called the shots".

"If corporates are putting pressure on their doctors to order health assessments or any other type of extra service, and the optional extras become mandatory, then there is a real problem there," he said.
"If they are actually putting pressure on the doctors, coercing them internally, to behave in a certain way in relation to billing services and generating services then that has to be stopped."
He said the GP sector was becoming increasingly corporatised and more guardrails were needed to regulate owners.
"It comes down to the fact that corporates actually rely on taxpayer-funded Medicare for their revenue streams.

"Legislatively, corporates do have responsibilities to their shareholders and investors. GPs have a responsibility to their patients. It's important that those two conflicting responsibilities are reconciled."
Questions about Bupa's management of practices follow the announcement in June of its biggest takeover yet, acquiring Partnered Health's 68 clinics nationwide.
'Clinical autonomy' in question

To comply with Medicare, GPs could only bill items like chronic care plans when they were "medically necessary", according to Royal Australian College of General Practitioners president Michael Wright.
He said the plans "were really designed" to encourage GPs to be more proactive with patients with complex conditions, and GPs should not be put under undue pressure to bill certain items.
"It's important that GPs know that they're available, but certainly they shouldn't be forced into any particular billing model."
"The financial autonomy of GPs is core to the successes of Medicare and our health system,"
Dr Wright said.

A Cubiko spokesperson said it respected the clinical autonomy of general practitioners, and its software helped practices meet strict Medicare eligibility rules "therefore reducing, not increasing, the risk of incorrect billing".
"Chronic disease is significantly under-managed in Australian general practice, and Cubiko's tools help practices identify patients who may have unmet care needs," they said.
Chronic care plans 'bugbear' of regulator
The potential abuse of the chronic care plans across the industry has angered Bill Coote, who headed the Medicare regulator, the Professional Services Review (PSR), between 2011 and 2016.

Doctors had long campaigned for the Medicare item to legitimately fund help for the growing burden of the population with chronic disease, said Dr Coote, a past secretary-general of the Australian Medical Association.
But during his time at the PSR, Dr Coote said he saw continued allegations of abuse of the billing items and said it was the "bugbear" of his existence at the regulator.
He said it had been "galling" to oversee cases of GPs submitting reams of plans and billed Medicare multiple times, but there was little or no information even written into the actual plans.
"There was certainly encouragement of practitioners to bill those items for anyone with a chronic illness,"
he said.
"So, the ones we saw tended to be the extreme ones … and their claiming numbers were really quite extreme."
Medical centres not registered for Medicare
In 2023, an independent review of Medicare Integrity and Compliance scrutinised the management of corporatised GP clinics.

The author of the report, health economist Pradeep Philip, noted "surprisingly" that medical centres do not need to be registered Medicare providers — even though they collect revenue from the scheme.
"Increasingly, practitioners note that they have less and less visibility and control over what is billed in their name," Dr Philip, of Deloitte Access Economics wrote.
Three years on, the Department of Health has confirmed that, despite recent law changes, there is still no requirement for medical centres and their operators to be registered with Medicare.
"Medical centres are private businesses and are required to comply with relevant legislation," it said.
In effect, it means GP employees can have their access to Medicare revoked for bad behaviour — but the centres themselves do not face the same risk for encouraging such conduct.
One penalty handed down
The PSR does have some powers to regulate body corporates like medical centres and hospitals.
However, it has handed down just one penalty to such an entity — only referred to in public documents as "a company", which was handed a $1.16 million fine in 2023 for "inappropriate practice".
It said the head of Medicare had referred other companies to the agency for investigation as well.
"However, these investigations have either resulted in no further action or have not yet been finalised," the PSR said in a statement.
The Department of Health said it was implementing key findings of the 2023 review and spending $147 million over four years to crack down on non-compliance and improve fraud detection.
Bill Coote said Bupa was clearly not giving due consideration to the legal and ethical position doctors were in, based on the email it sent.
"You get the impression it's written by someone who's much more focused on the bottom line."
